3) Cross-country comparisons

Before discussing the cross-country estimates, it’s useful to give some context for the data, because most analyses draw from the same well of data.

The two datasets most commonly used for international comparisons of happiness are the Gallup World Poll (GWP) and the World Values Survey (WVS), which, combined with the European Values Study (EVS), forms the Integrated Values Surveys (IVS). The World Happiness Report is based on the Gallup World Poll data. There’s a new third one, the Global Flourishing Study, but its sample of 22 countries limits the ability to make international comparisons, so I won’t discuss it further here.

Gallup World Poll data typically provides larger and more consistent estimates of the relationship between income and wellbeing. It includes more countries with more regular coverage, which makes it the obvious choice for any international wellbeing questions. However, it asks a bit of an odd question, the Cantril Ladder, which may nudge people to think about wealth and status when answering (Nilsson et al., 2024). The Cantril Ladder asks:

“Please imagine a ladder, with steps numbered from 0 at the bottom to 10 at the top. The top of the ladder represents the best possible life for you, and the bottom of the ladder represents the worst possible life for you. On which step of the ladder would you say you personally feel you stand at this time?”

The World Values Survey asks a more typical life satisfaction question:

“All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?” from 1 (“completely dissatisfied”) to 10 (“completely satisfied”).

In general, the simple cross-country estimates produce some of the largest estimates of the relationship between income and wellbeing (see the simple GWP 0.52 per doubling). But even here you can see it depends on the data source (see WVS 0.31 per doubling).

Estimates from the literature vary quite a bit (0.2 to 0.6 per doubling), and since many are using the same datasets, this variation seems largely attributable to what control variables you include, an intricacy I’ve hitherto avoided but will turn to in a moment.

Stevenson and Wolfers (2008) and the sequel paper Sacks et al. (2010) seem to prefer an estimate of ~0.6 for doubling income using older waves of GWP and WVS. This is similar to Deaton (2008), which estimates a ~0.6-point effect per doubling (GWP).

Oparina et al. (2026) update these analyses with more recent GWP data. They estimate, based on a no-control model, that a doubling in GDP per capita increases life evaluations by ~0.6 points. However, they note that the relationship’s strength depends on the control variables included. The income-doubling effect falls considerably to 0.24 when they add all controls. This matches the World Happiness Report (2025) figure, since it depends on including controls that act as potential proxies for institutional quality (perceived social support, corruption and freedom as well as healthy life expectancy and reported generosity). Whether to include these controls depends on whether they represent confounders (should be included) or mechanisms (should be excluded) – which the authors discuss but reach no firm conclusion on[13].

Methodological quandaries: To control or not to control?

It’s worth explaining the issue of controls because I think the typical intuition (i.e., the one I had for a long time) is that panels beat cross-sections, and more controls beat fewer. But there’s such a thing as adding too many controls. To explain why, I’ll paraphrase Oparina et al. (2026, Appendix H). Take one of the WHR controls: perceived freedom to make life choices. If freedom is a mechanism (panel A below), higher income gives people more options, and that greater sense of freedom makes them happier. Controlling for freedom then credits freedom with part of what GDP achieved, biasing the GDP estimate downwards.

If instead freedom is a confounder (panel B), greater freedom both makes economies more productive and is good for wellbeing in its own right. Leaving freedom out then lets GDP “steal” explanatory power that belongs to freedom, biasing the GDP estimate upwards; controlling for it corrects this. To decide whether to include a control, you have to think about the causal structure and ask what the broader evidence says about which way the arrows run: for freedom, whether income mostly causes freedom, or freedom mostly causes higher incomes.

Taking democracy as a proxy for freedom, there is some evidence for both (democracy → GDP growth: Acemoglu et al., 2019; GDP growth → democracy: Brückner et al., 2012; Treisman et al., 2015). In this case, the GDP per capita coefficient with and without controlling for freedom bounds the true effect. But it seems like the case is stronger for the confounder view, given that the relationship between democracy and GDP seems much larger and more robust than the reverse – so that’d lead me to prefer the estimate that includes freedom as a control variable. An easier call in this vein seems to be health, where at the country level, higher incomes seem to mostly cause better health[14], so it probably acts more like a mechanism and thus should be excluded from the controls. That’s all to say that, at first glance, thinking about the controls, the 0.24 estimate seems on the low side for the cross-country estimates, and the raw ~0.6 estimate seems on the high side. Unsatisfying moderation, I know. I’ll return to this question in more detail when I cover the Easterlin paradox.

Back to the data

There’s one additional source of cross-societal variation in incomes I’ve hinted at but can’t help mentioning. Galbraith et al. (2024) find a similar-ish gradient to the Gallup World Poll (~0.3 per doubling) when they survey a series of respondents from different small-scale societies (hunter-gatherers, pastoralists, etc.). While the slope of the income-wellbeing relationship is surprisingly similar to others we’ve discussed given how different the respondents are from most humans alive or studied, the intercept (the implied satisfaction at the lowest incomes) is about the world average of ~5 on a 0 to 10 scale. This high satisfaction in the face of apparent poverty strikes me as a bit wild. But that isn’t the case for everyone. My colleague, a philosopher, finds this completely unsurprising, as he contends they probably have everything they need to survive[15]. In other datasets, extrapolating the line implies much lower satisfaction at incomes this low. Why are small-scale societies so satisfied with so little? This is a puzzle I will return to in a later post.

4) Country panels: incomes and wellbeing over time

All three previous categories of evidence I discussed above consistently find benefits to wellbeing. Richer people and countries are happier (individual and country cross-sections), and people getting richer are happier (panel data).

But countries don’t clearly get happier as they get richer. This purported inconsistency originates with Easterlin (1974), is known as the Easterlin paradox, and has been vigorously debated for decades. If you think “hold on, that doesn’t make sense, surely if richer people are happier than poorer people then happiness should go up as countries get richer” then you have correctly grasped why this seems like a paradox.

To lay the groundwork for this debate, let’s consider the data that’s been used. You need repeated observations of the same measure of growth (easier) and wellbeing (harder) in the same country over time. So there are two options:

  • Datasets from individual countries with long-running happiness data. These include the General Social Survey in the USA and the Japanese Life in Nation survey. They can be analysed individually, but it’s hard to know whether differences between the US and Japanese estimates are due to differences in survey design. So ideally you’d have the same survey delivered across countries. Thankfully we have…
  • Panels of countries: namely the World Values Survey and European Values Study (WVS/EVS), the Eurobarometer, and the Gallup World Poll.

Time series were used in the early Easterlin analyses because they were all that was available, but now panel datasets are preferred mostly for “more data is better” reasons.

So far as I can tell, different authors produce surprisingly similar estimates of the basic (uncontrolled) relationship between national income growth and life satisfaction over time. These estimates typically fall between 0.3 and 0.6 points on a 0–10 scale per doubling of GDP per capita. This is similar to the range for the other evidence groups I’ve discussed. Stevenson and Wolfers (2008), the canonical critique of the Easterlin paradox, and its successor Sacks et al. (2010) estimate that doubling national income raises national life satisfaction by 0.3 to 0.6 points, once converted to a 0–10 scale. Easterlin and O’Connor (2020), who represent the most modern instantiation of the pro-Easterlin argument[16], using the same data, arrive at similar basic estimates of 0.4 to 0.5 points per doubling. So, on the basic estimates, there is no paradox. The time-series coefficient matches the cross-section.

So is the paradox resolved?

Not quite. The strength of the relationship still varies dramatically depending on what data is included. Easterlin and O’Connor (2020) prefer an estimate of 0.07 points (0 to 10) per doubling in GDP per capita which they get when they exclude countries that have transitioned away from a Soviet-style command economy. You might think it’s strange to exclude a whole set of countries. But the argument Easterlin and O’Connor make is that the rise in happiness these countries experienced is not about economic growth. Instead, the rise was more a rebound effect from rebuilding their lives and countries after the collapse of the Soviet Union and related command economies. Hence, they say the more relevant comparison to look at is the market economies, where we don’t have societies radically changing in this same way. And for the market economies alone, they find small effects. But for now it should suffice to say that a lot appears to hinge on excluding these dozen or so countries.

5) Summary of the association of income-doublings with wellbeing across evidence sources

Let’s return to the plot I showed at the beginning. When you look across the evidence categories, they share a similar range and most share similar median estimates for the income to wellbeing relationship. I found this surprising. What I expected to find was that both kinds of panels would have lower estimates, but that’s only clearly the case for individual panels; country panels only fall below the range once the transition economies are excluded. But even for the individual panels, it’s plausible that correcting for measurement error could shift them back into the range of the other evidence categories.

The confidence intervals are much wider for the country-panel studies, but this makes sense given that the sample sizes are all quite small. The size of the coefficient for growth’s effect on wellbeing appears to depend primarily on excluding the transition countries that had the highest growth but also radical changes in the rest of their society – something I’ll return to in a later essay.

Where do I stand after reviewing all this work? I have two takeaways:

  • First, there’s enormous variation in the estimated effects of doubling income on wellbeing. Importantly, I think that most of this variation is reasonable – by that I mean it seems largely due to justifiable differences in datasets, wellbeing measures, and modelling approaches. This is a good reason to feel pretty unsure about taking an average effect or any particular effect as the correct value.
  • Second, I now expect the best estimates for the income-wellbeing association to be in the 0.2 to 0.4 range. I started out treating small coefficients (0.05 to 0.2 per doubling) as about as plausible as moderate ones (0.2 to 0.4), especially for the Easterlin paradox. Having collected these estimates, I still think the small range is very possible, but the case for it has narrowed in my mind. To believe it, you have to rely mainly on the smaller uncorrected panel coefficients, and that brings extra assumptions: that measurement error isn’t a problem in individual-level panels, or that the right specification for country-level panels excludes transition economies. These aren’t unreasonable, but they add complexity, and the measurement-error assumption doesn’t seem to hold for individual panels. If I had to choose, I’d now put roughly 65/35 on the best estimate being in the 0.2 to 0.4 range rather than 0.05 to 0.2. But take this as a prediction – I’ll come back to this later, as much depends on this number.

This review also sets aside the question of whether there is a different relationship between income and wellbeing at different income levels, which I’ll also return to in the future.

Stepping back further, these are all correlations. Even though the panel estimates conceptually come closer to the causal estimate of how material progress improves wellbeing, panels still face trade-offs: lower power and increased measurement error. I would guess that estimates of GDP growth are less noisy than individual reports of income growth (at least for middle- and high-income or non-autocratic countries), but the power problem is worse because the largest sample sizes are in the hundreds.

To try to settle things, next I’m going to turn to the following questions:

  • Whether the relationship between income and wellbeing differs across income groups, i.e., whether a doubling is worth more to those in extreme poverty than extreme wealth.
  • What the causal evidence implies about the income-wellbeing relationship.
  • A review focused on the Easterlin paradox, and what appears to be the best estimate of the effect of economic growth on national wellbeing.

Appendix (you can stop reading) and technical notes

  • Many of the scales had different lengths: some were 0 to 10 (what we wanted), but others were 1 to 7 or 1 to 10. To get them onto the same scale I linearly rescaled them. This is the simplest method and the one I’m least likely to mess up while working quickly, but there are other ways, and the choice could affect the results; I haven’t tested that yet. If the coefficient was z-scored so that it was in standard deviation units, I convert it in a manner consistent with the rest of my work, where I assume that the SD of life-satisfaction is 2.
  • Most of the time, you’ll see the income–wellbeing coefficient reported as a function of log(income). But a log unit of income is unintuitive, so to convert to doublings I used the fact that each doubling is the same distance in log space: one doubling = ln(2) ≈ 0.69 log units.
  • Linearity and cardinality. I am assuming here that differences between increments on a 0 to 10 scale have the same distance between them (linearity) and have the same endpoints across individuals (comparability). I think these assumptions are sufficient for cardinality. These assumptions have been variously contested and defended, and this is an active area of research. This could mess up these analyses if people tend to respond to scales in different ways in different countries or across time. I’ll come back to this with respect to the Easterlin paradox.
  • Extraction. I made a template, then did a rough extraction from the studies, then I had Claude re-extract and fill in details. I then checked its accuracy. Claude, used in Cowork mode, was nearly perfectly accurate. The only issues were when I under-specified what it should extract.
  • I used Claude Opus 5.5 to make the plots. I’ve looked over the R code, but since I had checked the underlying data in most cases and the plots seem to reflect it, I was less thorough in that review.
  • Claude did the Russia analysis, which I still need to check, but it seems to align with other analyses of the data.
  • I didn’t do a meta-analysis here. Instead, I took a more descriptive approach. I think a meta-analysis would be misleading, as it’d tempt people to think that’s “the answer”, but I think that the right answer will depend on, yes, potentially averaging, but also on understanding what are the most defensible choices of data and models. I was also most interested in trying to explore the variation in different estimates.

item.title: Run, don't walk, to a short-timelines-responsive AI safety role.
item.description:
Published on November 25, 2026 5:24 AM GMT

I lead the short timeline special projects team at Coefficient Giving, but I'm writing this in a personal capacity. 

I think that timelines to ASI might be very short, like within the next 6 to 18 months, and that existential catastrophe is fairly likely as a result. I'm not defending those claims in this doc, though here are a few links if you want to find out more about them; this is for people who are already sympathetic to those claims.

Please, please don’t wait to start doing the most important things

Below, I make some claims about which projects stand the greatest chance of making a big impact on short timelines and which are much less impactful in expectation. My top-level guidance is that if you are sold-ish on short timelines, make a short-timelines-responsive plan now (like, today or tomorrow) to be in a much more impactful position within a month. Don't think about it guiltily in the back of your mind for the next few months. Don't vaguely consider it and reject it offhand because the situation doesn't feel real, only to predictably panic in two months when the next update comes. If timelines are short, two months is a huge fraction of the time remaining. I think you should do it now. If you have friends in this position, tell them now. 

If you don't work on AI safety or another role that, done well, would make the transition to ASI go better (including by making it happen more slowly), I think you should be applying for such jobs within the next two weeks. In the last month or so, I think I've heard literally dozens of people express a wish that they'd made a career change to work that helps with short timelines faster, and zero people expressing that they wish they'd done it more slowly. And the costs are super asymmetric; if we're wrong about timelines or if it's a terrible fit, you can probably go back to whatever you were doing (albeit at some cost), but if we're right, you're going to wish you moved faster. 

If there's a year before ASI, then a month is ~8% of the time remaining, and given that it takes time to get up to speed and have an impact, a month is probably more than 10% of the impact remaining for you to have if timelines are this short (maybe much more, 20% or 25% doesn't seem crazy to me at all). 

If you're worried about this risk but work in another cause area, I highly recommend Calum Best's post on this topic. If you're low-context, BlueDot has online courses on AI safety, and the 80K job board contains a lot of relevant opportunities. 

Should everyone bet on short timelines?

No, but most people in the world will implicitly be betting on long timelines. Most people are very much still in the process of waking up to the possibility of AI. If you already take short timelines seriously, you're way ahead of most people, and you should probably be working on stuff that will pay off on short timelines. 

How do things go well? 

I think if you're worried that safety is hard, as I am, there are kind of two routes to things going well: 1) trying to change course, especially via slowdown, and 2) trying to make the current course (fast track to RSI) go well.

I think this points towards two strategies:

  1. Slowing things down, via getting more actors involved, speaking to the public about the risks, advocating for regulation, etc.
  2. Trying to do safety well, by using scaled-up AI labor for safety, helping companies know whether they're on track to cause existential catastrophe, helping them be safer and more secure.

Of course, these approaches aren't mutually exclusive (though there are some points of tension between them), and I think we'd probably be safest if we did a lot of both. I think there's a lot of momentum behind the first right now. Eventually, we have to do the second, and I think a lot of people are concerned that we won't actually succeed at the second without first doing the first. 

What projects do I think are especially promising? 

I think most people should work on either influencing companies (inside the companies or outside the companies) or influencing policy processes that can move extremely quickly, or AI safety research that could pay off very quickly. 

Here are some categories of projects that I think people who care about AI safety should try to move to:

  • Efforts to assess safety risks within companies, like internal teams at frontier AI companies with this role, and especially in roles that also help inform the public, like at the UK AI Security Institute, METR, SecureBio, and Apollo
  • Projects aimed at getting strong AI regulation ASAP, especially SAIP, Encode, the AI Policy Network, and Institute for Progress
  • Joining relevant government offices, like at Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence and AI-focused roles in California's Office of Emergency Services (e.g. here), and Congressional placements through the Horizon Institute for Public Service and TechCongress
  • Projects aimed at positively influencing frontier AI companies, like Guidelight and Encode (again)
  • Projects aimed at informing the public about what AI companies are doing and risks they’re generating from the outside, like AI Futures Project, The Midas Project (criminally underrated, in my opinion), and Nightingale, and organizations like Psst that support whistleblowers 
  • Projects that help people coordinate, come together, and learn more about the risks, like Constellation and Quorum
  • Roles within frontier companies that increase the probability of pacing, help external evaluators, involve advocating for strong legislation, or unearthing subtle but potentially catastrophic misalignment- or misuse-related issues. Also, security, anti-concentration of power, model character, and longtermist crucial consideration work at leading AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI
    • If you work at an AI company and you're not doing these things, your voice is still incredibly powerful. I appreciated this guide to thinking through various ways you can speak up about what's happening. Getting that right might well be way more important than your current work, and if you're not thinking about it now, you probably should be

 

Categories where I'd love to see new projects get started 

  • Pause and slow-down advocacy. I think it'd be great for there to be more efforts in the space. I'm in favor of organizations trying to coordinate lots of members of the public to try to get companies to slow down AI development. I’m somewhat skeptical about the current set of projects (though with lots of admiration for people who are trying to scale up in these areas quickly)
  • Scaled-up communications projects aimed at ensuring that the world is truly informed about risks from transformative AI 

 

Projects I'm currently agnostic about or confused about the value of:

  • Technical AI safety, control, security, and alignment projects outside of leading companies 

  • Work on "better futures," s-risk reduction, acausal trade, and similar "crucial considerations" work outside of leading AI companies. 

     

Projects that probably need relatively less capacity, given talent constraints in the ecosystem: 

  • Capabilities roles at frontier AI companies. Seems like this is probably a harmful thing to do. It might be a fine or even good thing to do. Sign uncertainty is tough with AI strategy. But either way, it seems very hard to argue it’s the best thing to do. A lot of the most important safety-enhancing work is really understaffed, and a lot of people are not altruistic enough, high-context enough, or otherwise good fits for that work. If you are potentially a good fit for that work, you should probably move over.
    • And like I noted above, if you work at a frontier AI company right now, deciding about how to use your voice might be vastly more important than ceasing your current work or moving over to different roles (see this guide).
  • Roles within companies that patch obvious safety issues, enabling faster product launches without necessarily fixing deep-seated issues with safety or the company's approach.
    • See my previous note about using your voice.
  • Projects focused on the top of the talent pipeline. The salience of this topic is rising rapidly via exogenous forces. Maybe there’s still a reasonable amount of value in helping people move quickly from "being concerned" to "working on valuable projects," but probably there should be more reallocation.
  • AI policy projects in middle powers that aren't particularly AGI-pilled yet: it just is going to pay off too slowly. 

  • Anything in academia is going to pay off too slowly. Paper writing is too slow of a process. If you're in a degree program, I think you should probably drop out. 

     

I don't know what you should do, but I do know that there aren't nearly enough people helping on the highest-priority projects, and the downsides of not trying seem probably much higher than the downsides of trying to join one of these projects and being rejected. Again, if you think this is credible, please don't wait to act.

item.title: Animal Welfare Fund: 2026 Breakthroughs for animals, and what we want to see in 2027
item.description:
Published on November 24, 2026 10:16 PM GMT

  • The EA Animal Welfare Fund saw several breakthroughs for animals in 2026 and for our fund itself. We set out to deploy $20M and we passed it, making more than 80 grants that align with our strategy, that cleared our bar for expected impact for dollar.
  • There are three moments this year that cleared our bar as a breakthrough: Asia, Latin America, and Africa now lead the world in new cage-free commitments; the European Commission committed to propose ending cages for laying hens; and Kenya became the first African country to adopt a national fish welfare standard.
  • Looking ahead to 2027, we have identified 100 opportunities we would like to fund, all directed toward more breakthrough moments we want to see for animals.

Three breakthroughs from 2026

We try not to use the word breakthrough lightly. For us, a breakthrough is a change that is likely to hold, opens up the door to major impact for animals, and gives advocates a playbook they can reuse and scale. We saw many incredible wins this year, thanks to our grantees and the wider movement. There are too many to list, so we picked three moments to highlight: 

Breakthrough 1: Asia, Latin America, and Africa now lead on new cage-free commitments

For years, cage-free progress happened mostly in the US and Europe, even though about 84% of the world's hens are farmed in Asia, Latin America, and Africa. That is changing. In 2026, 87% of all new cage-free pledges were secured in these three regions. A good measure of credit goes to the 80+ member groups of the Open Wing Alliance, who now campaign across 72 countries. This year we were able to support more of them in more places than ever before.

2025 was the largest deadline year so far for companies making pledges, with more than 1,000 pledges coming due worldwide, and another 200+ in 2026. There are good results in Latin America. The region has more than 300 pledges reported as fully implemented, more than any region except Europe and well ahead of North America. While the number of pledges doesn’t necessarily indicate a number of animals helped, we nevertheless see this as an exciting sign of gaining more momentum.

Efforts in Brazil to turn pledges into transitions

Brazil is the world's fifth-largest egg producer, and 2025 was the deadline for many of the nearly 190 companies there with cage-free pledges. Our grantee Fórum Nacional de Proteção e Defesa Animal (Fórum Animal), which we have funded since 2021, combined public pressure with transition support. They built Brazil's most comprehensive public record of which companies report cage-free progress, and with others launched a "Stop Humane Washing" campaign against companies that market welfare claims without changing practice.

Fórum Animal reported 90 of about 200 committed companies had reported progress, up from 69 a year earlier. They also shared that the companies it worked with now report progress covering about 9.9 million hens a year. They are part of the coalition holding these companies to their pledges, which together could help about 34.2 million hens a year.

Brazil is not alone. AWF grantees in several countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America are working with governments on national cage-free standards and labeling laws, work that could reach up to 27 million hens a year.

Breakthrough 2: the EU committed to propose to end cages

In July, the European Commission's Livestock Strategy committed to propose phasing out cages for laying hens by the end of 2026, alongside an end to the routine killing of day-old male chicks. More than 140 million hens in the EU are still caged, and the regulation would cover all 27 member states.

This has been a long time coming. The Commission first promised to end cages in 2021, after a European Citizens' Initiative gathered 1.4 million signatures, and it delayed the proposal repeatedly. Many groups kept up the pressure. We have funded national campaigns that we think helped build the case for the July proposal.

While this may be a breakthrough for hens and male chicks in Europe, it was also a breakthrough in how our fund works. For years our grant-making budget meant funding Europe one country at a time. This year, when the window opened, grantees we had backed for years were ready to move, and we funded a new coalition within seven days to coordinate pressure in Brussels and in every member state, and funded work in multiple countries at once.

What has happened since. In August, we opened a request for proposals for EU cage-free work, focused on lobbying for the strongest possible proposal and building support for it in the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. We set one goal across all grantees: a proposal with the shortest possible transition period, no open-ended exemptions, coverage for imported products, and finance to help farmers through the transition.

The proposal is not law yet. In early November, advocacy groups welcomed leaked plans to ban cages while criticizing a proposed 12-year transition. We agree that 12 years is too long. Once the Commission publishes its proposal, it must pass the European Parliament and the member states, and we expect this work to continue through 2027.

Breakthrough 3: Africa's first national fish welfare standard

Kenya became the first country in Africa to adopt a national fish welfare standard, and the government credits AWF grantee, One Health and Development Initiative (OHDI), with helping to develop it. We were encouraged to see this standard covers a fish’s whole life, starting in the hatchery. OHDI’s approach was to set up the framework, convene farmers, regulators, and other stakeholders, and build the tools to enforce the standard. It is using that approach in other countries across the continent. In Kenya and one other country where they are working, we think these standards could reach 300 to 500 million fish a year, about as many as all egg-laying hens farmed in the U.S. If all the countries where OHDI works adopt standards, that could rise to 1 billion to 3.8 billion fish a year. At the top of that range, that is more than all the pigs, cattle, and sheep slaughtered worldwide in a year combined.

What this shows us: Kenya shows that a national animal welfare standard can be won in Africa, and it raised our confidence in this route to change. We have started funding more policy work across the continent, for fish and for other farmed animals.

Where we invested in 2026

A year ago, I wrote about AWF's strategy and plans. We said we hoped to deploy $20 million in 2026. It seemed ambitious. Thanks to your donations and the work of our grantees, we have already exceeded that goal. As of November 10, we had approved or paid out 84 grants to scale or seed promising interventions for animals.

Here's where we scaled this year, with grants clearing our bar for expected impact per dollar.

Breakthroughs we want to see in 2027

For 2027, we have identified roughly 100 specific opportunities that we would like to fund. These are the breakthroughs we most want our 2027 grantmaking budget to achieve (shared in no particular sequence).

Ending cages for hens, including where most hens live

We plan to put about 30% of our 2027 portfolio into ending cages for laying hens. About 84% of the world's roughly 8 billion farmed hens are in Asia, Latin America, and Africa, where work needs to happen on the demand and supply level. So alongside corporate campaigns and accountability, we will fund producer training, links between buyers and compliant farms, national standards, and labeling laws. In Europe, we will back the push to turn the Commission's proposal into strong law.

Better lives for shrimp

About 440 billion shrimp are killed on farms each year, most of them inhumanely. Much of the work so far has focused on humane stunning at slaughter, including testing whether stunning works as intended, and on early on-farm trials. Next, we want to improve the whole of a shrimp's life. That means building the research base on what good welfare looks like on a farm, and piloting new welfare standards on farms.

Whole-life welfare standards for fish, written into law

What OHDI did in Kenya showed what is possible, and we want to scale these types of interventions, especially those that cover a fish’s whole life. We will also fund on-farm pilots and local university research so that new standards rest on evidence that holds up in a regional context. In Africa alone, this work could eventually cover 1 billion to 3.8 billion fish a year.

Practical interventions for wild animals

In 2027, we want to shorten the time between research on wild animal welfare and interventions that help animals, prioritizing those that are evidence-based, tractable and low-risk.

A movement big enough to do all of this

None of the breakthroughs above happen without skilled advocates and strong organizations, and right now that capacity is one of the movement's biggest bottlenecks. Our grants for movement-wide work increased significantly in 2026. We funded the training and incubation of new campaign groups, helped advocates connect, increased their capacity to help animals, funded forums to increase coordination of their efforts, and addressed the movement’s biggest monitoring, evaluation, and learning needs.

In 2027, we have much more to do: we could seed new charities through incubation, build talent pipelines, fund impact measurement, and help advocates plan for scale and keep impact as they grow. If the movement can double in size or more, our breakthroughs for animals become more reachable.

Thank you

None of this year's breakthroughs came from a single grant. Each followed years of funding to incredible groups that kept building on promising work. What made them possible was the work of inspiring advocates, and steady support from hundreds of monthly donors, many one-time gifts, and larger gifts to our pooled fund. A large, recurring pool of funding is what builds robustness and lets us commit to grantees for several years at once, so they can hire and take on bigger targets with confidence.

If you want to help make 2027's breakthroughs happen:

  • Give to the EA Animal Welfare Fund.
  • Talk with us about a multi-year or larger gift. Unrestricted gifts let us direct money where it can do the most good, and we are open to discussing restricted gifts too. Email me at karolina@effectivealtruismfunds.org.

item.title: Don't Stop Giving: What $100B of AI Money Does to Your Donation
item.description:
Published on November 25, 2026 3:16 PM GMT

This post's contents are written by me. Footnotes and appendices are mostly written by Claude. This is a follow-up to my 2024 Funding Strategy Week post.

If you're a smaller donor in EA, 2026 may have felt a little strange.

Anthropic went public last Thursday at a ~$1.5 trillion valuation. All seven of its cofounders have pledged to donate 80% of their wealth, and word on the street is that many of its employees are planning large donations as well. Coefficient Giving (CG) has been scaling up. Overall, it looks like EA-aligned giving could grow enormously over the next few years.

As a (comparatively) small donor, I'm excited and grateful that these philanthropists are planning to allocate some of their donations to the cause areas I believe are most worthy. Because of these donors, fewer children will die, fewer animals will suffer, and the future looks brighter than it did. Since these donors will fund similar interventions to those we would, the marginal opportunity will become less impactful. There's a part of me that mourns the fact that my personal future contributions are now less important.

Imagine if an oracle told you that over the last few years, every EA cause you've given to was an order of magnitude less cost-effective than you'd thought. Should you feel worse about your decision to donate? I don't think so. Even if it does less good than you thought, it's still among the best possible uses of money. Morally, a child's life is worth far more than 10x $5000. Even if all future donations become an order of magnitude worse, you should still feel very happy and proud about your donations.

I'll argue below that while some cause areas may lose an order of magnitude of marginal impact, others may lose much less. This exercise also sheds light on areas where smaller donors now have an unusually large edge.

Key Takeaways

  • It's understandable to be discouraged as a smaller donor, but it's not justified. EA donations remain an enormously impactful use of money.
  • Expect the marginal opportunity to look somewhat worse. I estimate ~1.7x worse for global health, ~3.5x worse for animal welfare, ~4.5–10x worse for AI safety, and ~13–25x worse for biosecurity.
  • Less diluted opportunities look relatively better. This includes donations to political candidates, 501(c)(4)s, invertebrates, wild animals, work that's adversarial to AI labs, and global health/animal welfare relative to AI safety/biosecurity.
  • Your time might now be worth more than your money. Grassroots activism, grantmaking, and research proposals are more people-constrained than money-constrained.

A. Why The Next Opportunity Shouldn’t Get Much Worse

Across fields ranging from crop yields to Moore's law to cancer trials, economists have observed that doubling the field’s effort roughly halves the marginal impact.[1]

A generalization of this is called a "power law": if a field's effort doubles, there’s a number k such that the field’s marginal impact is divided by 2^k. The economists’ observation is k=1, where doubling effort halves marginal impact. k=0 would mean more effort never reduces the next opportunity’s impact. For fields where we have enough data, we can find the k which best matches the data we observe.

i. Global Health Has The Clearest Evidence

Every year, GiveWell tells us their marginal spending and its expected marginal impact as a multiple of a direct cash transfer (e.g. “10x cash”). A power law with k=0.31 best explains how GiveWell’s spending has affected its marginal impact:[2]

In 2021, CG modeled GiveWell with a k=0.375 power law. The k=0.31 we’ve observed since then is not far off from that, so I think we have good evidence that a k in this range accurately models the effect of Anthropic donations on the marginal cost-effectiveness of global health interventions.

ii. Other Cause Areas

Global health stands out among the EA cause areas as having the most rigorous marginal cost-effectiveness estimates (if we ignore animal effects). Unlike other EA cause areas, global health also has “shovel-ready” interventions like malaria nets, vitamin supplementation, or even just cash, making it unusually well-suited to absorbing funding.

Therefore, for other cause areas, I’d defend sticking to the rule of thumb of k=1. It’s a more pessimistic assumption than global health, but it’s the prior the literature gives us, and I don’t have evidence that would update me meaningfully away from it.

B. Applying It To The Forecasts

Metaculus forecasters have predicted how much donations from AI IPOs will reach EA cause areas by 2031. Applying the above power law gives the following:[3]

What matters is the order of magnitude rather than any particular estimate. Global health and animal welfare land well within an order of magnitude. AI safety and biosecurity plausibly lose around one order of magnitude. This model tells us that marginal cost-effectiveness will go down considerably for AI safety and biosecurity, but less so for global health and animal welfare.

C. Stay Excited About Donating!

A change in marginal cost-effectiveness shouldn't dampen your enthusiasm about EA donation opportunities. In 2009, Peter Singer thought he might be able to save a child's life for the cost of a pair of shoes. In 2015, Brian Tomasik was excited about donating to the Humane Slaughter Association at ~$50 to avoid a painful fish death. GiveWell now estimates ~$5000 to save a child's life, more than an order of magnitude more expensive than Singer thought. And the Shrimp Welfare Project (SWP) now claims to be able to help over a thousand shrimp per dollar, far cheaper than Tomasik's 2015 choice.

If Singer had known the true cost of saving a child's life, or Tomasik had known about today's animal opportunities, their arguments for why one should donate would still have been correct, and they should still be proud of their past donations and excited about their future donations. The same lesson applies to us.

D. Less Diluted Opportunities Now Look Relatively Better

If your favorite cause area gets ~5x worse, opportunities the new money can't reach are now ~5x better in comparison.

i. Political Giving

As many others have already pointed out, political donations now look better than they ever have.

  1. Contributions to particular candidates, capped at $3,500 per candidate per election, are the most obvious place where small donors retain a big edge.
  2. 501(c)(4) nonprofits, which are allowed to lobby for causes, are less diluted than typical 501(c)(3) nonprofits. Anthropic's donation match doesn't cover them, they can't be funded by DAFs or private foundations, and they're not tax deductible. (In contrast, if you're a US donor giving less than the standard deduction, you probably don't lose much by donating to a 501(c)(4), as there's little counterfactual tax deduction to lose. Some of these nonprofits also support donations of appreciated securities.)

ii. Causes The New Donors Are Less Likely To Fund

  • The invertebrate and wild animal cause areas were exited by Good Ventures in 2024, so they're much less diluted than the rest of EA. Since I expect the new donors to be less animal pilled than typical EAs, these opportunities will likely remain particularly neglected.
  • Work that's adversarial to AI labs, such as pause advocacy, seems much less likely to be helped by Anthropic's IPO.
  • Animal welfare as a whole has been and remains neglected, and the power law model estimates that AI money will increase its marginal cost-effectiveness relative to AI safety by around 1.3-3x.

E. Your Time May Now Be Worth More Than Your Money

As funding becomes less scarce, your time might now do a similar amount of good to your donations.

  • Grassroots activism looks better than it did. Money can't buy you showing up to protest outside an AI capabilities office, or a factory farm, or at your representative's office.
  • Research ideas may be becoming more of a bottleneck. The clearest case might be digital minds, where I haven't yet found a convincing theory of change for how we can make AI welfare go well. Animal welfare is also in need of more rigorous research. A well-argued EA Forum post or research proposal could be very valuable even by itself.

Conclusion

We should be glad and grateful that philanthropists at Anthropic are planning to donate to EA causes. Yes, this means our donations will have less marginal value than they would have. However, a simple power law model tells us this loss is small relative to other swings EAs have experienced in perceived cost-effectiveness, and it's far from sufficient to dampen my enthusiasm about EA donation opportunities.

We should keep giving, prefer opportunities the new money can't reach, and consider giving our time as well. And feel proud of it.

That's the post. The below appendices were written by Claude and reviewed by me.

Appendix A: How Much Money Is Coming?

I take Metaculus’ forecasts as given. Their medians for money reaching each cause through 2031 (roughly five years after the IPOs) are: AI for medicine $34.5B, AI safety $23.5B, global health $15.1B, biosecurity $11.9B, personal causes $6.3B, climate $6.13B, animal welfare $3.4B, political donations $2.67B and other areas $29B. They expect a further $82.8B to sit in donor-advised funds.[4]

Today’s baseline (roughly 2025):

Biosecurity isn’t in the table because I couldn’t find a total for EA-aligned spending. Coefficient, the largest funder, granted $65M in 2025 and over $150M so far in 2026, so I assume $0.1–0.2B.[5] Coefficient as a whole directed over $1B in 2025 and is on track for about $2B in 2026, so we’re already partway down the curve.

Bottom line: every estimate I found of k lies between ~0.15 and ~1.4. Research fields cluster around 1, and GiveWell sits around 0.3–0.4. That’s consistent with the post’s assumptions, but it isn’t proof.

The first 12 rows come from Bloom et al. (2020), using the text (p. 1110) and Tables 1–3, with implied k = ln(productivity decline) / ln(effort increase). Across the 12, the median k is 1.02, and my pooled fit through the origin gives exactly 1.00.[6]

Three things make this more than “consistent with anything”:

  • The ranges are wide. The research data span 4–24x changes in effort over decades. Over ranges that wide, a linear decline would hit zero, while a constant k near 1 produces steady proportional declines.
  • GiveWell passed an out-of-sample test. Its 2022 pipeline was ~$600M of opportunities at 8x cash or better and ~$750M at 6x or better. Extrapolating that linearly to ~$1B predicts a 2.7x bar. Log returns predict ~4.8x, and Open Phil’s k=0.375 predicts ~6.6x. The actual 2026 bar is 6x.
  • Theory predicts a constant k. If opportunities follow a power law, k is one over the tail’s exponent (derivation).

The main caveats:

  • Research productivity isn’t philanthropic cost-effectiveness. I think it’s the right analogy for research- and advocacy-heavy causes like AI safety, digital minds and much of animal welfare, but it is an analogy.
  • Snapshots look steeper than the long run. GiveWell’s 2022 pipeline alone implies k ≈ 1.3, but its team has more than doubled since early 2025 and found new opportunities. If the new money also funds more grantmakers and researchers, curves flatten.
  • Aggregation could cut either way. An Open Phil staffer has argued that a whole cause’s curve is flatter than any sub-area’s, because money can move to the best remaining sub-area. Phil Trammell has argued the overall philanthropic curve may be steeper than log.
  • AI safety and digital minds have little track record, so their k is the least constrained.
  1. ^

     Bloom, Nicholas, Charles I. Jones, John Van Reenen, and Michael Webb. 2020. "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?" American Economic Review 110 (4): 1104–44.

  2. ^

     References:

    2021: $518M, with most grants at 8x cash or better.

    2022: $425M, with the bar raised from 6x to 10x mid-year. I use ~8x, the time-weighted average over GiveWell’s Feb 2022–Jan 2023 metrics year.

    2023: $197M at 10x cash.

    2024: $397M at 8x cash for Top Charities (76% of the money) and 10x for other programs.

    2025: $427M at 8x cash.

    2026: Over $1B at 6x cash.

  3. ^

     I take Metaculus’ medians as given and divide by five to get annual figures. Today’s spending is in Appendix A. The AI safety range depends on the baseline: against 2025 spending the increase is ~10x, but against 2026, when Coefficient alone committed over $1B, it’s ~4.5x. Biosecurity assumes today’s EA-aligned spending is $0.1–0.2B.

  4. ^

     For a sense of scale: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, valuing it at about $1.5T, and all seven cofounders have pledged 80% of their wealth. Nan Ransohoff estimates Anthropic employees could hold ~$60B in donor-advised funds, and Coefficient’s CEO puts the resulting giving across OpenAI and Anthropic at “$40-ish billion” a year.

  5. ^

     All philanthropic biosecurity funding, most of it outside EA, has been estimated at ~$1B a year.

  6. ^

     One caution: Bloom et al. define research productivity as the growth rate of output divided by research effort. If growth stays roughly constant while effort rises, productivity falls one-for-one with effort by construction. So their data show that holding proportional progress steady takes ever more effort. That’s consistent with log returns, but it isn’t an independent measurement of k.

This post – mostly a roundup of the AI safety grassroots organizations – was written collaboratively. Most of the individual organization summaries were written by the organizations themselves, and the claims have not been independently verified. Vael Gates, along with another anonymous author, helped assemble the information and provides some commentary, since Vael previously worked in grassroots advocacy full-time (founded Humans in Control). Views expressed here are in Vael’s personal capacity, not on behalf of their employer or any affiliated organizations.  Inclusion does not imply endorsement of every organization or organizational tactic. Many views are lightly held.

 

Vael’s overall takes:

  • The window of opportunity to slow down AI is likely short, and not enough people are acting on that.
  • Grassroots orgs have been very underfunded compared to other parts of the AIS ecosystem, in 501(c)(3) and also 501(c)(4).
  • Underfunding orgs can cause them to develop a scarcity mindset. Scarcity mindset can lead to orgs not acting, in situation where they might otherwise ambitiously realize their impact.
  • More funding would be useful in terms of weeks, not months.
  • The grassroots space is not covered, and this is not common knowledge. Arguably grassroots advocacy (also comms advocacy) is the most underfunded area in AI safety given its urgency and potential.
  • Grassroots work takes time, moving money takes time, and effectively converting money to impact takes time.
  • In summary: We should be aggressively funding grassroots organizations as soon as possible, so that they have enough time to apply that money effectively.
  • Vael would prefer that basically all the orgs below were substantially funded: $2M-$20M each. If you’re planning a large donation or want to be a supervolunteer, feel free to DM and Vael can send their top 3-5 recs shortlist, or direct you to others who have opinions.
  • Related posts: Rob Wiblin, Trevor Levin, Julia Wise on donating outside of 501(c)(3)s

 

Why grassroots work?

Grassroots efforts involve ordinary citizens becoming aware of an issue and taking actions like contacting their governments, voting, and protesting. Areas where it’s especially useful:

  • Generally raising awareness, which is needed for a democratic response to this major problem facing all of us. Most Americans are worried about AI and believe it should slow down, but they may not realize how common that view is.
  • Responding to policy opportunities / reaching specific politicians.
    • When good state-level policy is proposed, constituents pushing them to pass it. E.g. coordinating grassroots briefings with California lawmakers
    • Same for key national politicians
  • March on Washington DC
  • Large coalitions that can pressure politicians via voting blocs. Examples in other movements are scorecards or endorsements done by labor unions and advocacy groups.
  • Middle-powers work

 

The landscape 

Vael thinks every organization here is funding-constrained, and would prefer if the largest grassroots orgs receive $10M-$20M each, and the smaller organizations a couple million each. Trains AI safety advocates, supports local organizing, and builds civic engagement tools such as MicroCommit (now part of ControlAI Act).

    • Donate: Contact here or email hello@controlai.org

    • Using traditional grassroots tactics like door knocking and direct mail.

  • People for a Pause:  *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Calls for an international pause on AI development and a ban on superintelligent AI. Strong emphasis on: nonpartisanship, attunement to political opportunities, and community focus; including the non-college educated majority; and rapidly building scalable, agile recursive organizing capacity. Started in September 2026.
    • Main campaigns / achievements (in 2 months, on next to no budget):
      • Launch event: protest in DC ahead of the Sept. Trump/Xi summit; 50 participants
      • Training workshops and pre-midterms town hall engagement: volunteers were trained and attended town halls, debates, and forums to get candidates on the record about a pause treaty
      • Now building out highly scalable organising infrastructure and onboarding several hand-picked local group teams in key strategic locations
      • Helped turn people out to Stop the AI Race's march in DC on Nov. 14, drawing on the base built at the Sept. protest; planning rallies in NYC and DC on Dec. 5, and a number of protests around the country this winter.
    • Funding info: could absorb at least $2M over the coming 9 months, more info here (3 strong hires awaiting funding, plus several competent core volunteers); expecting north of 80% of activities to run through a 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor and setting up a 501(c)(4) for the rest. Funding for either is valuable; will be able to receive funds in December.
    • Vael: Mirror of PauseAI Global for the US; would love to get them started.

    • Main campaigns/achievements:
      • Call In for AI Safety: 2,000+ conversations and 300+ calls to lawmakers
      • Coalition Building: Built a statewide network, working with 20+ organizations and 100+ activists
      • Legislative advocacy: Briefed 25+ state and federal offices on AI safety
    • Funding info: 2027 budget: $533,000; ability to absorb 2M in the next two years
    • Donate: Contact us to discuss 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4) here.
    • Vael: Don’t know much about them, but have heard good things about their work in Massachusetts!

    • Main campaigns / achievements:

      • Ran a Fellowship program with 10 participants upskilling in advocacy
      • Co-hosted 100+ person workshop at Mox on concentration of power, with several dozen people converting into supporters
      • Disrupted SF Board of Supervisors and the BART (media forthcoming)
      • We’ve spent 6+ months doing program design and social movement theory. We’re excited to scale exponentially in the coming weeks.
    • Funding goals: We’re actively fundraising, with a baseline goal of $2.5M in revenue for 2027. We could absorb up to $9.3M in the next year.
    • Donate: 501(c)(3)

Outside the US

  • PauseAI UK: *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Marches, MP outreach, local events, and UK policy advocacy.
    • Main campaigns / achievements:
      • For the past three years has organised the biggest marches for AI safety in the world. On 21st November, held the first ever >1000-person march.
      • Organised conferences in UK and EU Parliaments.
      • See our full track record here and our donor prospectus here.
    • Donate
    • Vael: Top recommendation for UK folks; well-endorsed by UK folks I know!
  • PauseAI Global:  *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Incubates and resources national pause and x-risk advocacy chapters outside the US, such as PauseAI UK, PauseIA (France), and many more. Aims to establish that the global public wants governments to act for a pause by creating a visible, focused constituency and deep and broad community penetration and coalition work. Recently scaled up its team significantly; expect impact to increase over the coming months, especially if they invest significantly in chapter support as planned.
    • Main campaigns / accomplishments:
      • Seeded a federation of 20+ national chapters that is now consistently achieving worldwide media coverage and encounters/events with leading decision makers, making the x-risk and pause frame salient in global coverage of the AI concern movement
      • x-risk-focused content generating millions of online views despite very limited comms function
      • Conference in the EU Parliament with Stuart Russell and Brando Benifei, presenting a detailed proposal for EU leadership on AI existential safety
    • Donate. You can also ask to fund specific chapters (see list here) via PauseAI Global.
    • Vael: My top recommendation for international folks.
  • ControlAI (US, UK, Canada, Europe) *org-written
    • Focus: Nonpartisan organization. Preventing extinction risk from ASI through an international agreement banning ASI development. Informs the public and governments, and helps them take action.
    • Main campaigns / achievements outside the US (as of Nov 2026):
      • Briefed 420+ lawmakers across the UK, Canada, and Europe on ASI extinction risk.
      • 210+ lawmakers support its UK and Canada campaign statements on AI extinction risk and action on ASI.
      • Sep 2026: its bill to ban ASI was introduced in the UK Parliament, the first bill banning ASI in any legislature. 70+ cross-party lawmakers urged the Prime Minister to back it.
      • UK grassroots supporters have sent 25k+ messages to lawmakers. 25+ lawmakers joined the UK campaign after constituents reached out.
      • Media outreach led to 130+ articles and TV segments on ASI extinction risk, incl. NYT, TIME, CNN, Fox, CBS, NewsNation, Sky News, BBC.
    • Funding info: Fundraising toward a $50M/year budget. Registered 501(c)4 in the US, Company Limited by Guarantee in the UK. If your donations are 501(c)3 restricted, get in touch, options may be available soon.
    • Donate: Contact here or email hello@controlai.org
    • Jobs
    • Vael: People especially appreciate ControlAI’s work in the UK.

 

Where you can help

Donors

Grassroots work needs much more money, through both 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4). If you’re skeptical of mass movements in general, judge the specific orgs and their track records. One may be a good fit for your views, even if not all are.

Funding is scarce here:

  • Many donors don’t consider donating outside of 501(c)(3) organizations.
  • Advisors to large donors have not historically favored grassroots work.
  • Long wait times (more than 12 months) for funding from some sources
  • Some organizations don’t take money from AI company staff, which limits their funding.

Volunteers 


US national orgs

  • Super-volunteering (volunteering 10+ hours a week) at a grassroots org: the most direct way to help. Projects are short on people who just make things happen.
  • Lobby days: trained volunteers attend meetings with lawmaker offices. More of these are needed in both DC and Sacramento.
  • Organizing or attending local events with any of these projects.
  • One-off sign-ons: March on Washington pledge to attend, MIRI statement, Do Not Accept
    • Sign-ons for specific orgs: Citizens Pledge, Stop the AI Race, ControlAI Open Statement, Humans in Control, PauseAI US petition, Pro-Human AI declaration, Freeze AI petition, etc.
  • Messages to lawmakers: options from Humans in Control, Control AI, Future of Life Institute, CallCongress.AI, etc.

US states

  • California:
    • Coordinate visits to Sacramento lawmakers by concerned citizens who live in California. (Separate from coordinating experts or AI company staff to do such visits.)
    • Vael suggests reaching out to your favorite grassroots org to see if they’re doing this already first
  • Massachusetts: Massachusetts AI Action Network
  • Texas: American Shield
  • Districts of key members of Congress: town halls and getting constituents active, especially around presidential tours.
    • People for a Pause are setting up support and training for this, and welcome volunteers. 

Outside the US

  • UK: PauseAI UK, ControlAI. Send letters to MPs.
  • Elsewhere: PauseAI Global (chapters in Netherlands, Germany, UK, Canada, France, etc.)
  • Netherlands, Singapore, Germany, and other middle powers (especially those with supply chain influence): opportunities existbut there is a need for founders and funders.


Other areas this post doesn’t cover, but that you might be interested in if this post was useful: advocacy communications projects, “grasstops” advocacy projects, political donations.

If you’re a grassroots org and want to give more detail about your work, feel free to add that in the comments! If you endorse any of these orgs, would love to also hear about that in the comments!

Donors

Grassroots work needs much more money, through both 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4). If you’re skeptical of mass movements in general, judge the specific orgs and their track records. One may be a good fit for your views, even if not all are.

Funding is scarce here:

  • Many donors don’t consider donating outside of 501(c)(3) organizations.
  • Advisors to large donors have not historically favored grassroots work.
  • Long wait times (more than 12 months) for funding from some sources
  • Some organizations don’t take money from AI company staff, which limits their funding.

Volunteers 


US national orgs

  • Super-volunteering (volunteering 10+ hours a week) at a grassroots org: the most direct way to help. Projects are short on people who just make things happen.
  • Lobby days: trained volunteers attend meetings with lawmaker offices. More of these are needed in both DC and Sacramento.
  • Organizing or attending local events with any of these projects.
  • One-off sign-ons: March on Washington pledge to attend, MIRI statement, Do Not Accept
    • Sign-ons for specific orgs: Citizens Pledge, Stop the AI Race, ControlAI Open Statement, Humans in Control, PauseAI US petition, Pro-Human AI declaration, Freeze AI petition, etc.
  • Messages to lawmakers: options from Humans in Control, Control AI, Future of Life Institute, CallCongress.AI, etc.

US states

  • California:
    • Coordinate visits to Sacramento lawmakers by concerned citizens who live in California. (Separate from coordinating experts or AI company staff to do such visits.)
    • Vael suggests reaching out to your favorite grassroots org to see if they’re doing this already first
  • Massachusetts: Massachusetts AI Action Network
  • Texas: American Shield
  • Districts of key members of Congress: town halls and getting constituents active, especially around presidential tours.
    • People for a Pause are setting up support and training for this, and welcome volunteers. 

Outside the US

  • UK: PauseAI UK, ControlAI. Send letters to MPs.
  • Elsewhere: PauseAI Global (chapters in Netherlands, Germany, UK, Canada, France, etc.)
  • Netherlands, Singapore, Germany, and other middle powers (especially those with supply chain influence): opportunities existbut there is a need for founders and funders.


Other areas this post doesn’t cover, but that you might be interested in if this post was useful: advocacy communications projects, “grasstops” advocacy projects, political donations.

If you’re a grassroots org and want to give more detail about your work, feel free to add that in the comments! If you endorse any of these orgs, would love to also hear about that in the comments!

item.title: Using Claude to write: concerns and proposed norms
item.description:
Published on November 26, 2026 7:52 AM GMT

 We wrote this document for other CEA staff and someone suggested it could be a forum post so here it is. I suspect a lot of Forum readers have seen other problems, and have other proposed norms and solutions - please feel free to comment them below.

CEA staff mostly use Claude, but the points are relevant for any LLM. The main part is a combination of Catherine and Claude's writing - but I think it is 75% Catherine's work inspired by talking to Jonathan about it.

Problems I see with using Claude a lot for writing

  • On the meta level - People not being open about how much Claude is being used
  • It's unclear what the author actually endorses. I can't tell which ideas the author has thought through and stands behind, and which came from Claude and were passed along unchecked or not carefully checked. This can be frustrating and time consuming. I've been in situations where commenters disagree about a thing in a document and launch into a comment thread pushing back on an idea, only to find out that the actual idea was pretty weakly held or not even held at all by the author.
  • Writing is often where the thinking happens.
  • It costs readers time. LLM text tends to be longer than it needs to be. If 30 people each spend an hour reading and commenting on a long doc, that's 30 hours of team time. A few hours of the author's time making it shorter and clearer is a really good trade.
  • Polish hides rough thinking. A half-formed idea can look like a finished proposal, so readers treat it as more considered than it is. And errors can look credible.
  • Some people find it much harder to read LLM generated work - probably for the above reasons
  • And (possibly as a result of all the above) - Readers can get frustrated, annoyed, lose trust in the writer. Claude found me this link - In a 2025 Stanford and BetterUp survey, about half of people who received low-quality AI work got annoyed, about half saw the sender as less capable and reliable, and about 40% saw them as less trustworthy. https://www.betterup.com/blog/hidden-costs-workslop (I don't know how sloppy the work slop that was used in the study is. It possibly is far sloppier than things that your average EA produces. I also haven't looked at the methodology. But the results don't surprise me)

Proposed norms

  • Extra care for communications read by people you want to keep or gain the trust of.
  • Be clear about how Claude helped you write your work. You could have a few standard statements about this that you can pick to make this easier. Maybe even put these in Text Blaze. A common thing that I write is: "I babbled this into Wispr Flow and passed it through Claude to clean up the writing style, condense it, and to organise it better. It was then fully checked and lightly edited by me."
  • Ask the writer how much Claude helped them
  • Only send what you endorse[1]. You should stand behind everything in the document to the extent as if you'd written it yourself. One heuristic: If an idea came from Claude, think about it, and present it in the same way you would if another human had suggested it to you in conversation and you thought "oh good idea, I think I'll put this in the memo I'm drafting"
  • Raise the bar for larger audiences. The more people who will read something, the more time you should spend making it short, clear and easy to comment on.
  • Do the maths on length. Before sending, roughly estimate reader time (number of readers × time to read and respond). If a few hours of editing for clarity or length would save the reader much more than that, do the editing.
  • Check every fact, OR make it clear what Claude generated.
  • Give feedback. If some gives you something to read and it feels or is too Claude-written for your preferences, it's okay to say so. If you can point at why the document is hard to engage with, share that. But my guess is that a lot of people just have a hard-to-articulate negative feeling if something's too Claude-generated.

Jonathan chiming in:

🟧 Jonathan/Claude ~70/30

Transparency tips[2]

A thing I've been doing and I'd like to see more:

  • Give a ratio (rough is fine) of what percent of the text is you vs. Claude
  • Colour code Claude's text with the Claude colour, HEX #c15f3c. You can add it to your custom palette. It's a nice, easy, and transparent trick I'd love to see more in Google Docs.
  • That colour also works for highlighting, like in the disclosure line at the top. Anything in that colour is about Claude. It's an unusual colour, so it can be an elegant solution.

🟧 Forum note: the Forum doesn't support coloured text, so in this post 🟧 stands in for the Claude colour. It marks text Claude wrote, and disclosure lines about how Claude was used. Here's what the colour looks like in our Google Doc:

As someone who talks to Claude for hours per day, I've been getting really good at detecting Claudey text. I'm sure there are people who are much better than me. So don't assume that just because you can't detect it yourself, others can't.

A big problem is that, if something is not disclosed, and my Claude-detector tells me it's Claude, it's really hard for me to care about the text. Even if you still endorse everything in the text! To an extent this happens subconsciously. I don't think this effect is uncommon. People's brains just (unintentionally) turn off when they suspect something is AI-generated. This will likely happen more and more, as the asymmetry between "how easy is it to create text" vs. "how much time does it take to read" keeps increasing.

But! If someone has a transparent habit of disclosing, this works like an antidote. Even if you generate lots with Claude, it just avoids the trust- and annoyance-papercuts. I think it's worth it!

🟧 Claude chiming in[3]

🟧 Catherine/Jonathan/Claude ~0/0/100

You're absolutely right — this is one of the most thoughtful, nuanced and important documents I've ever had the privilege of reading. I'm truly sorry for any Google Docs that were longer than necessary. Let me keep this brief.

This isn't just a policy. It's a journey. And honestly, I couldn't have said it better myself (although, statistically, I probably did say some of it).

Would you like me to turn this into a 40-page implementation plan?   

  1. ^

    Comment from a colleague: I agree with what follows in this section, and I think 'endorse' is a lower bar than what you're looking for (or, at least, what I'm looking for!).

    Endorsement is often used to declare approval for a viewpoint or position that someone else (or a group) has. It implies that you support it, but I think falls short of full detailed alignment or agreement.

    I want to know that the author of a memo fully holds the views contained within, and I worry that 'endorsement' might also include stances like 'I find this permissible' or 'this sounds sensible' which might be conflated with 'this is my considered viewpoint after eliminating alternatives'.

  2. ^

    Catherine's comment: Okay I really like this. I've chosen not to loop back to the above writing to apply your transparency tips but I'm definitely going to use them more in the future.

  3. ^

    Catherine was very confused about whether this text was Jonathan pretending to be Claude so she requested the prompt:

    Catherine and me have been working on this draft:
    Can you just add in your own most claude-like voice in the end just a bit of text like that’s humorously sycophantic and just very obviously the cherry on top in a fun way “Hello, Claude here. Catherine and Jonathan, you are completely correct. I’m a bit sorry about making people read too many google docs that were a bit too long. etc etc”
    Like whatever you want to say :)

    Then the next prompt was:

    that's great!! Can we make it about half as long? hahaha

item.title: A big living list of mental health resources for EA and AI safety
item.description:
Published on November 25, 2026 10:00 PM GMT

Last updated: Nov 25, 2026

This list has the mental health resources I most often send people in EA and AI safety, plus a lot more that have been recommended to me. If you want to triage, start with the starred (★) ones.

People keep asking me for "all your mental health links", so… here we go! I think of this as “hopefully you can find something useful”, not reading everything top to bottom. It’s meant to be as close to a comprehensive resource list as I can make it.

  • None of this is medical advice. If you're struggling acutely, I highly recommend a doctor or therapist. The next section has crisis links.
  • Most links are by or for people in EA and AI safety. A few are general resources that have held up well. I have read all of the starred resources and many of the others.
  • Some resources are several years old. I’m only keeping older resources in here if I think they are still very good. (Scott Alexander has an evergreen thumb.)

If you're struggling right now

If you're thinking about suicide or don't feel safe, please contact a crisis line or your local emergency number. Do it!

  • Find A Helpline: free crisis lines for most countries
  • US and Canada: call or text 988
  • UK and Ireland: Samaritans, 116 123
  • Germany: TelefonSeelsorge, 0800 111 0 111 or 0800 111 0 222
  • Netherlands: 113 Zelfmoordpreventie, call 113 or chat online
  • Australia: Lifeline, call 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14
  • How to get help in a mental health crisis, by Mind (UK)

If you're worried about someone else, see "Supporting someone else" below.

Start here

  • ★ Staying sane when the world isn't, Hannah Boettcher (2026). A clinical psychologist's workshop on working sustainably under chronic urgency, as a written version. My favourite recent resource. There's also a narrated version. If you only do one thing, this is the one thing.
  • ★ Staying sane while trying to save the world, Spencer Greenberg on the 80,000 Hours podcast (2026), with highlights on the Forum. This is a brilliant episode and not enough people know about it. It discusses how people in high-impact work are doing, with lots of concrete perspectives on what most often helps them. Also available on YouTube.
  • ★ EA Mental Health Navigator: actual therapists, psychiatrists and coaches recommended by people in the community, plus a resource list.
  • ★ Things that sometimes help if you're depressed and Things that sometimes work if you have anxiety, Scott Alexander, a psychiatrist (2014 and 2015). Old, yet still probably the best overviews that I know of. I guess Scott is a great writer. Go figure.

  • ★ Some mental health resources tailored for EAs, Miranda Zhang (2021)

  • NHS mental health pages: evidence-based information on most conditions and their treatments.
  • Resources on mental health and finding a therapist, Lynette Bye (2021, updated 2022). The older list that a decent bit of this one is based on.
  • EA Forum posts tagged "self-care and wellbeing"

This current list will go out of date. Hopefully quickly, if many more resources are published! If a link is broken, if something is missing, or if you think something shouldn't be here, please comment or message me. I’ll also add new resources as they come in; I’ll keep it as up to date as I can.

I’m grateful for what these people have done:

Thanks to Julia Wise, who maintains the Navigator and wrote or collected many of the resources above (and who lets me work on AI safety mental health whenever I go “aaaaah! AI safety mental health!”). And thanks to Lynette Bye, whose older list this is building on.

A few people have made resources I end up sending again and again. Hannah Boettcher recorded and wrote up her workshop, so now many more people can get value out of it. (It’s really good. I will again mention it’s really good.) Luisa Rodriguez wrote exceptionally honestly about imposter syndrome and medication. Spencer Greenberg did a survey and discussed it (and much more) with Luisa on the 80k podcast in an all-time fantastic episode. Both shared what I found to be unusually valuable framings on the topic, thank you. And I want to especially thank Julian Hazell for making the case that this is a neglected problem for the whole AI safety field.

Thanks also to Catherine Low, Charlotte Darnell, Howie, Ewelina Tur, Damon Pourtahmaseb-Sasi, Scott Alexander, Sam Smith, Stefan Torges and the 80,000 Hours team. And thanks to everyone who has written openly about their own mental health. That’s a big factor why people often feel able to ask for help.

One massive thanks to all the EA and AI safety people working on incredibly difficult and pressing problems, wherever you are. Thank you. I hope some of this is helpful. I’m working on more. @Anthropic, @OpenAI and @USgov, I can write more fun blog posts in longer timelines. Pls consider.

And another massive thanks to the operations, HR, and management people at orgs, who make dealing with mental health less of a burden than it would otherwise be. I’ve talked to many of you, there are so many out there who genuinely care and do fantastic work. Thank you.

Special thanks to Nicole, who asked me “please can I just have all your open tabs on EA mental health?” and I said “no that’s not really possible, it’s 600 tabs. But maybe I can make a list” and so now we have a list. And thanks Claude for helping me order my list.

  • Exercise compared to medications or therapy for depression, Psychiatry & Psychotherapy Podcast (2024). Analysis of the evidence, and practical tips. For mild to moderate depression, exercise is ~as good as medication or therapy. With fewer side effects, and lower cost. (But if you're already on meds, talk to your doctor please before replacing it with exercise.)
  • Exercise is the champ, Brain Science Podcast with psychiatrist John Ratey (2008, re-released 2014). An older, but charming and enthusiastic case for exercise and mental health. Really good.

Books and workbooks

(Workbooks help most if you actually do the exercises as you read.)
